claims.text: Increasing local lattice distortion by adjusting refractory-element ratios is the primary mechanism governing the superior high-temperature strength and altered thermoelastic behavior of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Refractory high-entropy alloys with intentionally enhanced lattice distortion will have higher yield strength than alloys with lower distortion.
Refractory high-entropy alloys with intentionally enhanced lattice distortion will exhibit a distinct temperature dependence of elastic modulus.
As-cast or homogenized refractory high-entropy alloys contain existing elemental segregation.
As-cast or homogenized refractory high-entropy alloys possess inherent local lattice distortions.
Systematic adjustment of refractory-element ratios can control the degree of local lattice distortion.
Keeping casting, homogenization, and annealing identical provides a controlled comparison of composition-dependent behavior.
The range 1200–1400 °C represents service-relevant high-temperature conditions for the proposed refractory high-entropy alloys.
Solute misfit induced by composition changes produces local lattice distortion.
Changes in local lattice distortion may be accompanied by elemental segregation.
Enhanced local lattice distortion modifies the local energy landscape and strengthens dislocation–solute interactions.
Stronger dislocation–solute interactions increase the resistance or critical strain required for dislocation motion.
Increased resistance to dislocation motion leads to higher yield strength.
Enhanced lattice distortion alters the temperature sensitivity of elastic moduli.
Higher-distortion samples will show a statistically significant increase in yield strength relative to a low-distortion baseline.
Higher-distortion samples will show a modified, potentially less conventional, temperature dependence of elastic modulus relative to the baseline.
Using a low-distortion baseline processed identically controls for processing variability.
The proposed mechanism is applicable strictly at 1200–1400 °C under constant strain rate and controlled environmental conditions.
The qualitative association between lattice distortion, strength, and thermoelastic response is supported only indirectly, and segregation or other microstructural factors may contribute.

Failure to observe either a statistically significant yield-strength increase or a changed elastic-modulus temperature dependence in higher-distortion alloys would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
